subject: PE
overview: Third-grade PE is taught in 30-minute daily sessions that always start with the dynamic warm-up and end with a cool-down. Demonstrate each skill with 2–4 short cues, let the child practice many repetitions while you give one specific correction at a time, then check with the week's skill check. Keep a fitness and skill log all year so the child compares to their own baseline, not to others; stress safety rules, soft landings, and fair play in every game.

weeks.prep: Clear an open, flat play area free of furniture, rocks and holes; set 4 cones as boundaries. Make sure the child has sneakers and a water bottle. Write 4–5 PE safety rules on a card (stay in boundaries, keep personal space, stop on the signal, use equipment only as taught, tell an adult if hurt) and pick a stop signal (whistle or 'Freeze!').
misconceptions: Thinking a warm-up means static stretching cold muscles. A warm-up should be moving (dynamic) to raise heart rate and body temperature; hold-still stretches belong in the cool-down.
Thinking the cool-down is optional or means sitting down right away. Slowing down gradually and then stretching helps the heart rate come down and muscles relax.

days.guide: Read the safety rules card aloud and have the child repeat each rule. Show 'personal space' by having them spin slowly with arms out (their bubble). Play 5 minutes of bubble-space tag: everyone moves with arms out and must not pop anyone's bubble; freeze on your signal and check that they stop right away.

questions.q: What is personal space?
questions.a: The space around your body you can reach with arms out (your 'bubble'); in PE you keep your bubble from touching anyone else's.

questions.q: What do you do when you hear the stop signal?
questions.a: Stop moving right away, freeze, and look and listen to the adult.

days.guide: Demonstrate each of the 6 moves (jog, high knees, arm circles, skips, lunges, butt kicks) once, then do them together for about 30 seconds each. Watch that lunges keep the front knee over the ankle and that the child moves under control. Ask how their body feels at the end (warmer, breathing faster).

questions.q: Name 3 moves in our dynamic warm-up.
questions.a: Any 3 of: jog, high knees, arm circles, skips, lunges, butt kicks.

questions.q: Why do we warm up before exercise?
questions.a: To raise heart rate and body temperature and loosen muscles and joints so they work better and are less likely to be injured.

days.guide: After a short jog, lead 4–5 static stretches (quad stretch, hamstring reach, calf stretch against a wall, arm-across-chest, triceps), holding each 15–20 seconds with no bouncing. Have the child breathe slowly and say 'stretch, not pain.' Ask them to explain why we cool down.

questions.q: How long do you hold a cool-down stretch, and should you bounce?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds, holding still and breathing slowly — no bouncing.

questions.q: Why do muscles need a cool-down?
questions.a: It lets the heart rate and breathing slow down gradually and helps warm muscles relax and stay flexible, which reduces stiffness.

days.guide: Have the child lead the warm-up, then play 15 minutes of freeze tag inside the cones (tagged players freeze until a free player tags them). Remind them of tagging gently on the shoulders or back. Finish with the cool-down stretches.

questions.q: Where is a safe place to tag someone?
questions.a: A gentle touch on the shoulder, arm or back — never a push, grab or tag on the head or face.

questions.q: What comes first and last in our PE session?
questions.a: Warm-up first; cool-down last.

days.guide: The child leads the family through all 6 warm-up moves, calling out each one and showing correct form. Then they name 3 safety rules without the card. Use the assessment rubric below.

questions.q: Name 3 PE safety rules.
questions.a: Any 3, e.g., stay inside the boundaries, keep personal space, stop on the signal, use equipment the right way, tell an adult if you are hurt, wear sneakers.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for leading the warm-up: 4 = leads all 6 moves (jog, high knees, arm circles, skips, lunges, butt kicks) in order with correct form, clear voice and about 30 seconds each, and names 3 safety rules; 3 = leads 5–6 moves with minor form slips and names 3 rules; 2 = needs prompts for several moves or names only 1–2 rules; 1 = cannot lead the warm-up without the adult doing it.

weeks.prep: Gather a timer or phone stopwatch and make a fitness/heart-rate log (columns: date, activity, heart rate before, heart rate after). Plan 6 circuit stations with simple equipment (jump rope or jumping jacks, wall push-ups, curl-ups, sit-and-reach, plank hold, jog laps).
misconceptions: Mixing up muscular strength and muscular endurance. Strength is how much force a muscle can make once (a hard push); endurance is how many times or how long it can keep working (many curl-ups).
Counting the pulse with the thumb. The thumb has its own pulse; use the index and middle fingers on the side of the neck or the thumb side of the wrist.

days.guide: Teach the 5 components of health-related fitness: cardiorespiratory (heart-lung) endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. For each, act out an exercise together (jog in place, wall push-up, 10 curl-ups, toe-touch reach, and for body composition talk about eating well plus being active). Have the child match each card to its exercise.

questions.q: Name the 5 components of health-related fitness.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.

questions.q: Which component does a sit-and-reach stretch work on?
questions.a: Flexibility.

days.guide: Show the child how to find the pulse with two fingers on the side of the neck (carotid) or inside the wrist below the thumb (radial). Sit quietly 2 minutes, count beats for 15 seconds while you time, then multiply by 4. Record resting heart rate in the log.

questions.q: You counted 22 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate per minute?
questions.a: 22 × 4 = 88 beats per minute.

questions.q: Which fingers do you use to find your pulse, and why not the thumb?
questions.a: The index and middle fingers; the thumb has its own pulse and can confuse the count.

days.guide: Take a 15-second resting count, then do 2 minutes of jumping jacks and immediately count again. Record both numbers and the difference in the log. Ask the child to describe what else changed (breathing faster, feeling warm, sweating).

questions.q: Your heart rate was 84 before and 140 after jumping jacks. How much did it go up?
questions.a: 140 − 84 = 56 beats per minute higher.

questions.q: What else changes in your body when you exercise hard?
questions.a: You breathe faster and deeper, feel warmer, and may sweat.

days.guide: Set up 6 stations (e.g., jog laps = cardio, wall push-ups = strength, curl-ups = endurance, sit-and-reach = flexibility, plank = endurance, jumping jacks = cardio) and work 45–60 seconds at each with a short rest. At each station the child says which fitness component it builds.

questions.q: Which component does jogging laps build?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (heart and lungs).

questions.q: Which component do push-ups build?
questions.a: Muscular strength (and muscular endurance when you do many).

days.guide: Review the log together. Ask the child to explain in their own words why the heart rate rose during exercise, then check the log for completeness.

questions.q: Why does your heart rate rise when you exercise?
questions.a: Working muscles need more oxygen and energy, so the heart pumps faster to send more oxygen-rich blood to them (and you breathe faster to get more oxygen).

questions.q: What happens to your heart rate after you stop and rest?
questions.a: It slowly goes back down toward your resting heart rate.

weeks.assessment_key: Heart rate log check: proficient log shows a resting heart rate correctly calculated (15-second count × 4, typically about 70–110 bpm for this age), a post-exercise rate that is higher, the difference subtracted correctly, and a sentence explaining that the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygen to working muscles. 4 = all parts correct; 3 = one math slip; 2 = numbers recorded but no explanation; 1 = log incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a tape measure or yardstick, a box about 12 inches high for sit-and-reach (or tape a yardstick to the floor), a mat, a stopwatch, and mark a half-mile route (or a 20-meter lane with cones for the PACER; free PACER audio is online). Print a fitness log with baseline columns. Warm up before every test.
misconceptions: Thinking the tests are a competition with others. These scores are a starting point to compare against yourself later in the year.
Doing push-ups or curl-ups as fast as possible. FitnessGram-style tests use a steady cadence (about one every 3 seconds) with correct form; reps with bad form do not count.
Writing a goal like 'get better.' A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

days.guide: Warm up, then teach curl-up form: knees bent, feet flat, arms straight with fingertips sliding along the mat about 3 inches, at a slow cadence (one every 3 seconds) until form breaks. Then 90-degree push-ups: straight body, lower until elbows bend to 90 degrees, at the same cadence. Record both counts.

questions.q: What does a 90-degree push-up mean?
questions.a: You lower your body until your elbows are bent at a right angle (upper arm parallel to the floor), keeping your body straight.

questions.q: Which fitness component do curl-ups test?
questions.a: Abdominal muscular strength and endurance.

days.guide: After warming up, do the back-saver sit-and-reach: one leg straight with the foot flat against the box, the other knee bent; reach forward slowly 4 times and hold the 4th for 1 second; measure inches, then switch legs. For the shoulder stretch, reach one hand over the shoulder and the other up the back — record yes if fingertips touch, for each side.

questions.q: Why do we warm up before the flexibility test?
questions.a: Warm muscles stretch farther and are less likely to be strained.

questions.q: Should you bounce to reach farther?
questions.a: No — reach slowly and smoothly; bouncing can pull a muscle and does not count.

days.guide: Warm up, then time the half-mile walk/run (or run the PACER, counting laps until the child misses two beeps). Remind them to pace themselves rather than sprinting at the start. Record the time or laps and cool down with walking and stretches.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you sprint at the start of the half-mile?
questions.a: You will tire out quickly; a steady pace lets you finish with your best time.

questions.q: Which fitness component does the half-mile or PACER test?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) endurance.

days.guide: Explain SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Look at the baseline scores and help the child choose one area and write a goal, e.g., 'I will do 15 curl-ups by the March retest by doing curl-ups 3 times a week.'

questions.q: What does SMART stand for?
questions.a: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

questions.q: Is 'I want to be stronger' a SMART goal? Fix it.
questions.a: No — it is not measurable or time-bound. Example fix: 'I will do 10 push-ups by March by practicing push-ups 3 days a week.'

days.guide: Set up the weekly fitness log (date, activity, minutes, how it felt). Have the child fill in this week's entries and copy their goal at the top. Check that all baseline scores are recorded.

questions.q: How will the log help you reach your goal?
questions.a: It shows how often you practice and lets you see progress toward your goal over time.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline check: the log should show (1) curl-up count, (2) push-up count, (3) sit-and-reach in inches for right and left, (4) shoulder stretch yes/no for each side, (5) half-mile time or PACER laps, and (6) a written SMART goal. Proficient goal example: 'I will improve my PACER from 12 to 18 laps by the spring retest by jogging 15 minutes three times a week.' Score: 4 = all scores recorded and goal has all 5 SMART parts; 3 = goal missing 1 part; 2 = scores missing or goal vague; 1 = no goal.

weeks.prep: Set up a 'yard' lane about 20–30 yards long and 6–8 cones for pathways; have upbeat music ready. Preview the definitions: hop = one foot to the same foot; leap = one foot to the other with a long flight; skip = step-hop alternating; gallop = same foot leads forward; slide = sideways gallop.
misconceptions: Confusing a hop and a jump. A hop takes off and lands on the same one foot; a jump takes off and lands on two feet (or two to one / one to two).
Galloping and sliding look the same. In a gallop you face forward with one foot always leading; in a slide you move sideways, chest facing forward, without crossing the feet.

days.guide: Demonstrate each locomotor skill and have the child do each one across the yard: walk, run, hop (each foot), skip, gallop (each lead foot), slide (both directions) and leap. Give one cue per skill (e.g., skip: 'step-hop, swing arms').

questions.q: What is the difference between a hop and a leap?
questions.a: A hop takes off and lands on the same foot; a leap takes off on one foot and lands on the other with a long stretch in the air.

questions.q: In a slide, which way do you face?
questions.a: You face forward (chest to the front) while moving sideways, feet not crossing.

days.guide: Lay cones in a straight line, a curve and a zigzag. Have the child travel each pathway with a different skill (walk the straight, skip the curved, slide the zigzag). Then call out a pathway and a skill and let them choose the cones.

questions.q: Name the 3 pathways we practiced.
questions.a: Straight, curved and zigzag.

questions.q: Draw or describe a zigzag pathway.
questions.a: A path of straight lines with sharp turns back and forth, like the letter Z repeated.

days.guide: Model run-to-leap: 3–4 running steps, then take off on one foot and land on the other, then keep running. Then skip-to-slide: skip 4 times, turn sideways and slide 4 times without stopping. Practice each 5 times, cueing 'no stopping between skills.'

questions.q: What does a smooth transition mean?
questions.a: Changing from one movement to the next without stopping or stumbling.

questions.q: When you run into a leap, which foot do you land on?
questions.a: The opposite foot from the one you took off on.

days.guide: Build an obstacle course with 4–5 parts (e.g., zigzag run through cones, leap over a pool noodle, hop to a cone, slide to the finish). The child completes it 3 times, trying to make each change smooth.

questions.q: Which skill did you use to get over the noodle, and why?
questions.a: A leap (or jump), because it carries you up and over the object.

days.guide: The child designs and performs a 4-skill sequence (e.g., skip → gallop → slide → leap), saying it aloud first, then performing it twice. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Tell me your 4 skills in order.
questions.a: Any 4 correct locomotor skills named in the order performed, e.g., 'skip, gallop, slide, leap.'

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for 4-skill locomotor sequence: 4 = performs 4 different locomotor skills with correct form and smooth transitions (no stops), repeats it the same way; 3 = 4 correct skills with one pause or stumble; 2 = 2–3 skills correct or several stops; 1 = cannot show a sequence of skills.

weeks.prep: Gather tape or chalk for a start line, a measuring tape, chalk for the vertical jump (or sticky notes), and draw a hopscotch grid (1–10). Jump on grass or a soft surface.
misconceptions: Landing with straight, locked legs. Land on the balls of the feet and bend hips, knees and ankles to absorb force ('land like a spring').
Keeping arms still. Swinging the arms back then forward and up adds force and distance.

days.guide: Teach 'quiet landings': jump in place and land softly on both feet with knees, hips and ankles bent, as if landing on eggshells. Practice 10 small jumps and 5 jumps off a low step, checking that you can barely hear the landing.

questions.q: How do you land safely after a jump?
questions.a: On both feet (balls of the feet first), with knees, hips and ankles bent to absorb the force, arms forward for balance.

questions.q: Why does a quiet landing mean a good landing?
questions.a: It means your legs bent and absorbed the force instead of slamming down.

days.guide: Teach the standing long jump: feet shoulder-width behind the line, crouch and swing arms back, swing arms forward and jump out, land on both feet. Measure from the line to the back of the heel closest to the line. Do 3 jumps and record each.

questions.q: Where do you measure a long jump to?
questions.a: From the start line to the back of the heel (the landing mark closest to the line).

questions.q: Jumps of 42, 47 and 45 inches — which is your best?
questions.a: 47 inches.

days.guide: Have the child stand sideways to a wall, reach up with chalky fingers and mark standing reach. Then crouch, swing arms and jump, marking the highest point. Measure between the two marks. Do 3 tries.

questions.q: Your reach mark is 54 inches and your jump mark is 63 inches. What is your vertical jump?
questions.a: 63 − 54 = 9 inches.

questions.q: Should you take a running start for this test?
questions.a: No — jump from standing with two feet, using a crouch and arm swing.

days.guide: Play hopscotch: toss a marker, hop on one foot on single squares and land on two feet on side-by-side squares, skipping the marker square, then turn and come back. Add variations: hop only on the left foot, or jump with feet crossed.

questions.q: In hopscotch, when do you land on two feet?
questions.a: On the squares that are side by side (and at the turn-around).

questions.q: Is a single-square move a hop or a jump?
questions.a: A hop — one foot to the same foot.

days.guide: Review the jump log. Have the child do 2 long jumps — one without arms, one with a full arm swing — measure both and explain the difference.

questions.q: How do your arms help you jump farther?
questions.a: Swinging the arms back and then forcefully forward and up adds momentum and force that carries the body farther.

questions.q: What should you do with your legs when you land?
questions.a: Bend the knees, hips and ankles to absorb the force.

weeks.assessment_key: Jump measurements check: proficient record shows 3 standing long jumps measured to the nearest inch from line to heel with the best circled, a vertical jump calculated as jump mark minus reach mark, and soft two-foot landings with bent knees on every trial. 4 = all measurements correct and safe landings; 3 = one measurement error; 2 = missing a test or landings stiff; 1 = record incomplete.

weeks.prep: Make a 10-foot tape line on the floor (or use a curb or low 2x4 beam no higher than a few inches). Lay cushions or a mat nearby for falls. Have a stopwatch to time 5-second holds.
misconceptions: Holding the breath and looking down. Keep breathing, look at a fixed point ahead, and tighten the belly to stay steady.
Thinking fewer body parts touching makes a balance easier. Fewer points of contact (a smaller base of support) make it harder; a wide base is more stable.

days.guide: Call out balances on different body parts: 4 points (hands and knees), 3 points (lift one arm), 2 points (one hand, one foot, or two feet), 1 point (one foot, arms out). Hold each 5 seconds while the child counts. Teach 'eyes on a spot, tight tummy.'

questions.q: Which is harder to hold: a balance on 4 body parts or on 1? Why?
questions.a: On 1, because the base of support is smaller, so it is easier to tip over.

questions.q: What helps you hold a balance?
questions.a: Looking at one spot, tightening your stomach muscles, arms out to the sides, and breathing steadily.

days.guide: Walk forward heel-to-toe along the line, then backward (toe reaching back), then sideways with slide steps. Add arms out to the side. Finish each pass with a controlled dismount: step off and land with bent knees.

questions.q: Where should your eyes be when walking the line?
questions.a: Looking ahead at the end of the line or a spot in front, not down at your feet.

questions.q: How do you dismount safely?
questions.a: Step or jump off with control and land on both feet with bent knees.

days.guide: Show counterbalance (partners face each other, hold wrists, lean back together) and counter-tension; also try back-to-back sitting down and standing up together. Stress slow movement and talking to each other.

questions.q: In a counterbalance, why do you both need to lean equally?
questions.a: Each partner's weight holds the other up; if one leans more or lets go, both lose balance.

questions.q: What should partners do before letting go?
questions.a: Agree and come back to standing slowly together, then release.

days.guide: The child chooses 3 balances (e.g., stork stand, V-sit, 3-point bridge) and links them with smooth transitions. Have them write or draw the sequence, then practice it 3 times.

questions.q: Name your 3 balances and how many body parts touch in each.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., stork stand (1 foot), V-sit (seat), bridge (2 hands, 2 feet = 4).

days.guide: The child performs the 3-balance sequence, holding each balance still for 5 seconds with smooth transitions. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What is a base of support?
questions.a: The body parts touching the ground that hold you up.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for balance sequence: 4 = 3 different balances, each held still for 5 seconds, smooth transitions, controlled start and end; 3 = all 3 balances but one wobble or brief pause; 2 = holds only 1–2 balances for 5 seconds; 1 = cannot hold balances.

weeks.prep: Use a tumbling mat, old mattress or soft grass; make a gentle incline by putting a cushion or folded blanket under one end of the mat. Clear the area. Parent spots every forward roll. Skip forward rolls if the child has any neck or back problems.
misconceptions: Rolling on the top of the head. Tuck chin to chest so the back of the head and shoulders touch the mat, never the top of the head.
Opening the body mid-roll. Stay in a tight ball (hold shins) so the rounded back rolls smoothly.

days.guide: Lie the child on the mat with arms stretched overhead and body straight like a pencil. They roll sideways the length of the mat 5 times each direction, keeping legs together and arms up.

questions.q: What shape is your body in a log roll?
questions.a: Long and straight like a pencil, arms overhead, legs together.

days.guide: Teach the egg roll: kneel in a tight tuck with forearms and head tucked, roll sideways onto the back and back to knees. Then rocking chair: sit in a tuck holding shins, chin to chest, rock back and forth on a rounded back 10 times.

questions.q: Why do we practice rocking chairs before a forward roll?
questions.a: To learn to keep a rounded back and tucked chin so we roll smoothly and safely.

questions.q: Where should your chin be during a roll?
questions.a: Tucked to your chest.

days.guide: On the incline mat: squat at the high end, hands on the mat shoulder-width, chin to chest, push with the legs and roll over the back of the head and shoulders, finishing in a squat. Spot with one hand on the back of the neck/head and one under the hips/thighs. Repeat 5–8 times.

questions.q: What part of your body touches the mat first in a forward roll?
questions.a: The hands, then the back of the head and shoulders (never the top of the head).

questions.q: Why use a gentle incline?
questions.a: Gravity helps you roll over easily, making it safer while you learn.

days.guide: The child plans a 3-part routine: a balance (held 3–5 seconds), a roll (log, egg or forward), and a jump with a soft landing. Practice the transitions and finish with a still end position.

questions.q: How should you land the jump at the end of your routine?
questions.a: On both feet with bent knees, arms up or forward, holding still.

days.guide: The child performs the routine. Then ask them to explain 'chin to chest' and show it. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why do we say 'chin to chest'?
questions.a: It rounds the back and keeps the top of the head and neck off the mat so the neck is protected during the roll.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for tumbling routine: 4 = balance held still, roll performed with chin tucked and rounded back, jump landed softly on two feet, smooth transitions, explains 'chin to chest' protects the neck; 3 = all parts safe with one wobble or pause; 2 = roll unsafe (head not tucked) or a part missing; 1 = cannot complete safely.

weeks.prep: Get a jump rope (beaded or PVC rope works well). Size it: stand on the middle with one foot; handles should reach the armpits. Jump on a flat, non-slip surface (driveway, gym floor). Prepare a jump log and pick a slow and a faster song.
misconceptions: Turning the rope with big arm circles. Elbows stay close to the sides and the rope turns from the wrists.
Jumping too high or double-bouncing. Jump only an inch or two off the ground, on the balls of the feet, one jump per turn.

days.guide: Size the rope (stand on the middle; handles to the armpits). Hold both handles in one hand and swing the rope at your side to feel the rhythm from the wrist. Then hold one in each hand and turn the rope over the head and let it stop in front of the toes, step over, repeat 10 times.

questions.q: How do you know your rope is the right size?
questions.a: Standing on the middle with one foot, the handles reach about to your armpits.

questions.q: What part of your arm turns the rope?
questions.a: The wrists (with elbows close to your sides).

days.guide: Practice the basic bounce: feet together, small jump on the balls of the feet as the rope passes under. Do 5 sets of 20-second tries with 30-second rests. Cue 'small jumps, quiet feet, wrists turn.'

questions.q: How high should you jump in the basic bounce?
questions.a: Just an inch or two — enough for the rope to pass under.

questions.q: Why do we rest between sets?
questions.a: Jump rope is hard work for the heart and legs; rest lets you recover so you can keep good form.

days.guide: Do 3 trials of counting consecutive jumps without a miss. Record each number and circle the best in the jump log.

questions.q: Trials were 14, 22 and 19 jumps. What is your best? What is the difference between best and worst?
What counts as 'consecutive' jumps?
questions.a: Jumps in a row without the rope stopping or a miss.

days.guide: Jump to a slow-tempo song, trying to land one jump per beat. Then switch to a faster song. Talk about which was easier and why.

questions.q: What do you need to change when the music gets faster?
questions.a: Turn the rope faster with the wrists and make smaller, quicker jumps to stay on the beat.

days.guide: Warm up, then do 3 trials to try for a new personal best and record it. Ask the child to compare this week's first count to the best.

questions.q: How did practice change your count?
questions.a: Answer should compare numbers, e.g., 'I went from 14 to 30 because I kept my jumps small and turned with my wrists.'

weeks.assessment_key: Jump log check: proficient log lists 3 counted trials on Day 3 with the best circled, a Day 5 personal best, and a sentence comparing them using numbers and a reason (e.g., better timing, wrist turning, smaller jumps). Form check: rope sized to armpits, elbows in, wrists turning, small two-foot jumps. 4 = all present; 3 = log complete but reason vague; 2 = missing trials; 1 = no log.

weeks.prep: Have the jump rope, a timer, a trick checklist (skier, bell, side swing, alternate foot) and the heart-rate log from week 2 with the resting heart rate.
misconceptions: Swinging the whole body for skier or bell. Keep feet together and move only a few inches side to side or front to back, with small jumps.
Thinking the side swing needs a jump. In the side swing, both handles go to one side and the rope swings past without jumping over it.

days.guide: Draw a line on the ground. Teach the skier: feet together, jump side to side over the line without the rope, then with the rope, one jump per turn. Complete 3 sets of 10.

questions.q: In the skier, which direction do your feet move?
questions.a: Side to side (left and right), feet together.

days.guide: Teach the bell: feet together, jump forward and back over the line like a bell swinging. Then the side swing: bring both hands together and swing the rope on one side of the body, then open the hands and jump the next turn.

questions.q: How is the bell different from the skier?
questions.a: In the bell you jump forward and backward; in the skier you jump side to side.

questions.q: Do you jump during a side swing?
questions.a: No — the rope swings beside your body; you jump on the next turn after you open your arms.

days.guide: Teach the alternate-foot step: jog in place, one foot lands per turn of the rope (right, left, right, left). Practice without the rope first, then try for 20 in a row.

questions.q: In the alternate-foot step, how many feet land on each turn of the rope?
questions.a: One foot each turn, switching feet like jogging.

days.guide: Take resting heart rate (15 s × 4). Jump for 1 minute (any tricks), then immediately take the pulse again and record. Compare the numbers.

questions.q: Resting was 80 bpm; after jumping you counted 36 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate after jumping, and how much higher?
Which fitness component does jumping rope build most?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (also muscular endurance in the legs).

days.guide: The child performs 3 tricks in a row (e.g., skier, bell, alternate foot) while a family member checks each off on the checklist.

questions.q: Name the 3 tricks you performed.
questions.a: Any 3 of: basic bounce, skier, bell, side swing, alternate foot.

weeks.assessment_key: Trick checklist: check each trick performed correctly for 5 or more consecutive jumps: basic bounce (feet together, small jumps), skier (side to side), bell (front to back), side swing (rope swings at side, no jump), alternate foot (one foot per turn). 4 = 3 tricks in a row smoothly; 3 = 3 tricks with a stop between them; 2 = 2 tricks; 1 = basic bounce only.

weeks.prep: Get a long rope (about 14–16 feet) and two turners, or tie one end to a fence or post. Pick a song about 30–60 seconds long with a steady beat for the routine. Look up the traditional jump-rope chants 'Teddy Bear, Teddy Bear' and 'Cinderella' (short, public-domain playground rhymes).
misconceptions: Running in at the wrong moment. Use the 'front door' (the rope comes over the top toward you): wait until the rope hits the ground in front of you, then follow it in.
Standing near the end of the rope. Jump in the middle of the rope where the arc is highest.

days.guide: Turners swing the rope in big, steady circles. Teach 'front door' entry: stand beside a turner, watch the rope hit the ground, and run in to the middle just after it passes. Jump 5 times, then exit by running out diagonally toward the opposite turner's side right after a jump.

questions.q: Where in the long rope should you jump?
questions.a: In the middle, where the rope is highest.

questions.q: When do you run in?
questions.a: Right after the rope hits the ground and moves away from you, so you have time to get to the middle before it comes around.

days.guide: Teach the rhymes and their actions (e.g., 'Teddy Bear' — turn around, touch the ground). Jump while chanting and doing each action on the beat. Turners keep a steady rhythm.

questions.q: Why do we chant rhymes while jumping?
questions.a: The rhyme keeps a steady beat so the jumper and turners stay in time, and it adds actions to practice.

days.guide: Help the child pick 4 tricks (e.g., basic bounce, skier, bell, side swing) and decide how many jumps of each (e.g., 8 each) to fill about 30 seconds of music. Write the plan in order.

questions.q: If you do 8 jumps of each of 4 tricks, how many jumps is your routine?
questions.a: 8 × 4 = 32 jumps.

questions.q: Write your routine order.
questions.a: Any 4 tricks in order with counts, e.g., 8 basic, 8 skier, 8 bell, 8 alternate foot.

days.guide: Rehearse the routine 5 times with the music. After each run, choose one transition to smooth (e.g., keep turning the rope while changing tricks).

questions.q: How do you change tricks without stopping the rope?
questions.a: Keep the wrists turning at the same speed and change your feet on the next jump.

days.guide: The child performs the routine for family and then names one trick to keep improving and how.

questions.q: What trick will you keep improving, and what will you practice?
questions.a: Any trick plus a specific fix, e.g., 'bell — keep feet together and jump smaller.'

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for jump rope routine: 4 = 4 different tricks performed in planned order for about 30 seconds, mostly on the beat, with 2 or fewer misses and smooth restarts; 3 = 4 tricks with 3–4 misses or one long stop; 2 = 2–3 tricks or many misses; 1 = basic bounce only. Long rope: entered, jumped 5 and exited (yes/no).

weeks.prep: Gather 10–20 tennis balls (or rolled socks indoors). Tape a target about 2 feet square on a garage or fence wall with the center about 3 feet high; mark a throw line 15 feet away. Find an open field for distance throws. Make a 4-cue checklist.
misconceptions: Stepping with the same foot as the throwing arm. Step with the opposite foot (right-handers step with the left).
Facing the target squarely and pushing the ball. Start with the non-throwing side toward the target so the hips and shoulders can rotate.

days.guide: Teach the 4 cues: 1) side to the target, 2) arm way back, 3) step with the opposite foot, 4) follow through across the body. Have the child say the cues and shadow-throw (no ball) 20 times while you watch each cue.

questions.q: If you throw with your right hand, which foot steps forward?
questions.a: The left foot (the opposite foot).

questions.q: Name the 4 overhand throwing cues.
questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step with opposite foot, follow through.

days.guide: From the 15-foot line, the child throws 20 tennis balls at the wall target using all cues. Tally hits on paper.

questions.q: You hit the target 7 times out of 20. How many misses?
questions.a: 20 − 7 = 13 misses.

days.guide: In an open field, throw for distance: run-up optional, big step with the opposite foot, full follow-through. Mark the best throw with a cone and pace or measure it.

questions.q: What should you change to throw farther?
questions.a: Take a bigger step, rotate hips and shoulders, and throw with more force with a full follow-through (aim a little upward).

days.guide: Partners take turns: one throws 5 times while the other checks each cue on the checklist. Then switch and discuss.

questions.q: Your partner stepped with the same foot. What cue do you give?
questions.a: 'Step with the opposite foot' — the foot on the other side from the throwing arm.

days.guide: The child explains all 4 cues, then throws 10 at the target and compares the hit rate with Day 2.

questions.q: Monday: 7 of 20 hits. Today: 5 of 10 hits. Which day was more accurate?
questions.a: Today — 5 of 10 is half; 7 of 20 is less than half (10 would be half).

weeks.assessment_key: Throw cue checklist (score each throw yes/no): side to target, arm back, opposite-foot step, follow through. Proficient = all 4 cues on at least 4 of 5 observed throws, plus a target tally recorded for Day 2 and Day 5 with a correct comparison. 4 = all 4 cues consistently; 3 = 3 cues consistently; 2 = 2 cues; 1 = 0–1 cues.

weeks.prep: Gather a beanbag, a soft playground ball and a tennis ball. Make 'reach and give' and 'thumbs/pinkies' cue cards. Open space for partner catch and jogging.
misconceptions: Trapping the ball against the chest. Catch with the hands, reaching out and 'giving' (pulling the ball in) to soften it.
Using the same hand position for every catch. Above the waist: thumbs together; below the waist: pinkies together.

days.guide: Self-toss a beanbag a little above head height and catch with hands, saying 'reach and give' (reach out to the object, pull it in softly). Do 20, then repeat with a ball.

questions.q: What does 'reach and give' mean?
questions.a: Reach your hands out toward the ball, then bend your elbows and pull it in to soften the catch.

questions.q: Where should your eyes be when catching?
questions.a: On the ball all the way into your hands.

days.guide: Toss to the child at different levels. High balls: hands up, thumbs together. Low balls: hands down, pinkies together. Mix levels and call out the hand position after each catch.

questions.q: A ball is coming at your knees. How do you hold your hands?
questions.a: Pinkies together, palms up/forward.

questions.q: A ball is coming above your head. How do you hold your hands?
questions.a: Thumbs together, fingers up.

days.guide: Play partner catch starting 5 steps apart; after each 3 successful catches in a row, the child takes one step back. Count the farthest distance reached.

questions.q: Why do you step back only after 3 good catches?
questions.a: It makes sure you are successful at one distance before making it harder.

days.guide: The child jogs across the yard while you toss the ball slightly ahead of them. They catch without stopping. Switch roles.

questions.q: When catching on the move, where should the ball be thrown?
questions.a: Slightly ahead of the runner so they can catch it without stopping.

days.guide: Play partner catch and count the best streak of consecutive catches in 3 tries. Record the best.

questions.q: Streaks of 12, 18 and 15. What is your best streak?

weeks.assessment_key: Catching streak record: proficient = best streak of 10 or more consecutive partner catches at about 10 feet using hands (not trapping), with correct thumbs/pinkies hand position at high and low levels. 4 = 15+ catches and correct hand positions; 3 = 10–14; 2 = 5–9 or frequent trapping; 1 = fewer than 5.

weeks.prep: Gather a playground ball, a flying disc, a small/junior football and 4–6 cones. Set a straight cone path for the receiver.
misconceptions: Throwing to where the runner is now. A lead pass goes to where the runner will be.
Flicking the disc with a straight arm and wobble. Curl the arm across the body, step toward the target, and snap the wrist keeping the disc flat.

days.guide: Set a straight cone path. The child jogs it while you throw a lead pass to the space ahead; switch so the child throws to you. Talk about aiming at the space ahead.

questions.q: What is a lead pass?
questions.a: A throw to the space ahead of a moving teammate so they can catch it without slowing down.

days.guide: Teach the backhand: grip with the thumb on top and fingers underneath on the rim, stand sideways, curl the disc across the body, step toward the target and snap the wrist, releasing it flat. Play catch 15 minutes; catch with a 'pancake' (one hand on top, one under).

questions.q: How should the disc be when you release it?
questions.a: Flat (level with the ground), with a wrist snap to spin it.

questions.q: What is a pancake catch?
questions.a: Catching the disc between one hand on top and one hand underneath, clapping it.

days.guide: Teach the football grip: fingers on the laces, ball held near the back, throw over the shoulder with the overhand cues and let the ball roll off the fingers for a spiral. Throw to a stationary partner, then to a moving one.

questions.q: Where do your fingers go on the football?
questions.a: On the laces, toward the back half of the ball.

days.guide: Watch a partner make 5 throws. The child gives two specific compliments ('Great step with the opposite foot') and one cue ('Follow through toward me').

questions.q: What makes feedback specific?
questions.a: It names exactly what was done well or what to fix, like 'Your arm went way back,' not just 'Good job.'

days.guide: Run a 10-pass moving drill: receiver jogs the cone path, thrower makes a lead pass; count completions out of 10.

questions.q: You completed 7 of 10 passes. How many were incomplete?

weeks.assessment_key: Moving passing drill scoring: count completions out of 10 lead passes. 4 = 8–10 completions with passes thrown ahead of the receiver; 3 = 6–7; 2 = 4–5 or passes thrown behind; 1 = 0–3. Also note whether the child gave 2 specific compliments and 1 cue on Day 4.

weeks.prep: Collect 10 plastic bottles (add a little sand or water so they stand), 2–3 balls, tape for a throw line, and the week 11 target tally. Graph paper for the accuracy graph. For hit-the-pin, set a bottle or cone 'pin' in front of each player.
misconceptions: Faking means throwing for real. A fake is a pretend throw motion to make a defender move, then you pass to the open side.
Thinking fair play only matters when winning. Fair play means following rules, taking turns and being honest whether winning or losing.

days.guide: Set 10 bottles in a triangle or line. The child throws overhand from the line, using all 4 cues, and counts how many throws it takes to knock all 10 down.

questions.q: Which cues help you hit the bottles?
questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step with the opposite foot, follow through toward the target.

days.guide: Play monkey in the middle: two throwers pass while the middle player tries to intercept. Teach the fake (start a throw one way, pass another way) and quick passes. Rotate after an interception.

questions.q: Why use a fake?
questions.a: It makes the defender move the wrong way, opening space for a pass.

questions.q: What kind of pass is hard for the monkey to catch?
questions.a: A quick, accurate pass away from the defender — over or around them, not right at them.

days.guide: Re-test 20 throws at the week 11 target from 15 feet. Make a bar graph comparing week 11 hits to today's hits.

questions.q: Week 11: 7 hits. Today: 12 hits. How much did you improve?
questions.a: 12 − 7 = 5 more hits.

days.guide: Play hit-the-pin: each player protects a pin; take turns throwing to knock down others' pins. Set fair-play rules first (take turns, no throwing at people, honest calls).

questions.q: What should you do if your pin is knocked down?
questions.a: Admit it honestly, say 'Nice shot,' and follow the game rule (reset or rotate).

days.guide: Skill check: observe 5 throws and 5 catches; score each throw on the 4 cues and each catch on reach and give / correct hand position.

questions.q: Show me how you'd catch a ball thrown at your belly button and one at your ankles.
questions.a: Belly button: thumbs together (or hands ready to pull in); ankles: pinkies together.

weeks.assessment_key: Throw/catch skill check: Throws (5) — 1 point per cue observed on each throw (side, arm back, opposite step, follow through), max 20. Catches (5) — 1 point each for a clean hands catch with correct hand position. Proficient = 16+ throw points and 4 of 5 catches. 4 = 18–20 and 5/5; 3 = 14–17 and 4/5; 2 = 10–13 or 3/5; 1 = below.

weeks.prep: Use a playground ball or junior basketball (size 5) inflated to bounce to about waist height. Flat surface such as a driveway; set 6 cones about 5 feet apart for Friday.
misconceptions: Slapping the ball with the palm. Push the ball down with the finger pads, wrist and fingers relaxed.
Looking at the ball. Keep eyes up so you can see where you are going and where others are.

days.guide: Demonstrate dribbling: knees bent, push the ball down with the finger pads at waist height, ball beside (not in front of) the body. Dribble 30 times with the right hand, then 30 with the left.

questions.q: What part of your hand pushes the ball?
questions.a: The finger pads (fingertips), not the palm.

questions.q: How high should the ball bounce?
questions.a: About waist high or lower.

days.guide: Dribble walking to a cone 20 feet away, turn, switch hands and walk back. Repeat 4 times. Cue 'ball slightly ahead and to the side.'

questions.q: Why switch hands at the turn?
questions.a: To keep the ball on the side away from where you are turning and to practice both hands.

days.guide: Dribble while jogging the length of the driveway. The ball is pushed out in front a little more and bounces a bit higher than walking. Jog back and repeat 5 times.

questions.q: How is a running dribble different from a stationary one?
questions.a: You push the ball a little farther in front of you so you can move forward without kicking it.

days.guide: While the child dribbles in place, hold up fingers; they call out the number without stopping. Then do the same while walking.

questions.q: Why practice dribbling with your eyes up?
questions.a: So you can see teammates, defenders and where you're going while still controlling the ball.

days.guide: Set the 6-cone course. The child dribbles around each cone and back without losing control. Time it if desired.

questions.q: What counts as losing control?
questions.a: The ball bouncing away, being caught/held with two hands, or stopping the dribble.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble course rubric: 4 = completes 6-cone course with finger-pad dribble, ball at waist height or lower, eyes mostly up, no loss of control; 3 = one loss of control or eyes mostly down; 2 = two or more losses; 1 = cannot dribble continuously.

weeks.prep: Ball and 6–8 cones set in a zigzag (cones alternating about 4 feet left and right). Agree on 'red light/green light' signals.
misconceptions: Crossing over high. A crossover bounce should be low (below the knee) and quick so a defender can't steal it.
Stopping the dribble to tag in dribble tag. Players must keep dribbling the whole time; if you pick up the ball you must restart.

days.guide: Teach the crossover: dribble low with the right hand, push the ball in a V-shape across the body to the left hand, bounce below the knee. Practice 3 sets of 20.

questions.q: Where should the ball bounce in a crossover?
questions.a: Low, in front of your body (a V shape), below the knees.

questions.q: Why keep the crossover low?
questions.a: A low, quick bounce is harder for a defender to steal.

days.guide: Dribble through the zigzag cones, switching to the outside hand (the hand farther from the cone) at each one.

questions.q: If a cone is on your left, which hand should you dribble with?
questions.a: Your right hand — the hand away from the cone or defender, protecting the ball.

days.guide: Play red light/green light: green = speed dribble, yellow = slow, red = stop and control the ball dribbling in place (or hold it). Practice quick changes.

questions.q: How do you dribble fast?
questions.a: Push the ball farther ahead and a bit higher, and run.

days.guide: Play dribble tag in a small area: everyone dribbles; the tagger tries to tag others while dribbling. Lost balls must be recovered before playing on.

questions.q: In dribble tag, how do you protect your ball from a tagger?
questions.a: Keep your body between the tagger and the ball and dribble with the hand away from them.

days.guide: Skills check: 10 crossovers in place, one zigzag pass through the cones switching hands, and a speed change on call.

questions.q: Which hand do you use after a crossover from right to left?
questions.a: The left hand.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble skills check (1 point each, 6 total): crossover low and controlled (1) for 10 in a row (1); zigzag with hand switches (1) and no loss of control (1); speed change on 'red/green' (1) with control maintained (1). 4 = 6; 3 = 5; 2 = 3–4; 1 = 0–2.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball (size 3 or 4) and 6–8 cones; open grass. A stopwatch for Friday's timed course.
misconceptions: Kicking the ball far ahead when dribbling. Use small touches so the ball stays within a step of your feet.
Using only the toes. Use the inside and outside of the foot for control; toe kicks are hard to control.

days.guide: Teach toe taps (lightly tap the top of the ball with alternating soles, 50 times) and inside-foot touches (pass the ball between the insides of both feet, 50 times). Keep on the balls of the feet.

questions.q: Which parts of the foot do you use to dribble a soccer ball?
questions.a: The inside and outside of the foot (and the sole to stop); small touches, not toe pokes.

days.guide: Dribble through a line of cones using small touches with both feet, keeping the ball close. Go 4 times through.

questions.q: How far should the ball be from your feet while dribbling?
questions.a: Close — within about one step so you can control it.

days.guide: Dribble in an open space; when you shout 'Stop!' the child puts the sole of the foot on top of the ball to stop it. Practice 10 times.

questions.q: How do you stop the ball quickly?
questions.a: Step on top of it lightly with the sole of your foot.

days.guide: Play soccer dribble tag: the child dribbles in a marked square while a defender tries to touch or kick the ball out. Teach shielding: body between the defender and the ball.

questions.q: What is shielding?
questions.a: Keeping your body between the defender and the ball to protect it.

days.guide: Set the cone course. Time the child dribbling through and back; do 2–3 trials and record the best time.

questions.q: Trial times were 28, 25 and 26 seconds. What is your best time?
questions.a: 25 seconds (lowest time is best).

weeks.assessment_key: Timed foot-dribble course: record best of 3 times. Form rubric: 4 = small touches with both feet, ball stays close, weaves every cone without missing; 3 = mostly controlled, one missed cone or ball runs away once; 2 = big kicks or several missed cones; 1 = cannot complete course with the ball.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, a small goal or two cones 6 feet apart for the target, 15-foot mark, open field.
misconceptions: Kicking with the toe for passes. Pass with the inside of the foot for accuracy; shoot with the laces (top of the foot).
Planting the support foot far behind the ball. Plant the non-kicking foot beside the ball, toe pointing to the target.

days.guide: Teach the inside-foot pass: plant foot beside the ball pointing at the target, turn the kicking foot out, strike the middle of the ball with the inside, follow through. Make 30 passes with a partner about 15 feet apart.

questions.q: Where does your plant foot go for a pass?
questions.a: Beside the ball, toes pointing toward your target.

questions.q: Which part of the foot passes the ball?
questions.a: The inside of the foot.

days.guide: From 15 feet, kick 20 passes through two cones 6 feet apart and tally successes. Narrow the gap if it's easy.

questions.q: You got 14 of 20 through. How many missed?

days.guide: Teach the laces shot: approach at an angle, plant beside the ball, toe pointed down, strike with the laces and follow through toward the goal. Take 15 shots.

questions.q: Which part of the foot do you shoot with?
questions.a: The laces (top of the foot) with the toe pointed down.

days.guide: Partner jogs across the field; the child passes ahead of them (lead pass) with the inside of the foot.

questions.q: Where should you pass to a moving teammate?
questions.a: Into the space in front of them, so they can run onto it.

days.guide: Kicking check: 5 inside-foot passes through the cones and 5 laces shots on goal; score each on the cues.

questions.q: Why is the inside of the foot more accurate than the toe?
questions.a: It's a bigger, flatter surface, so the ball goes where you aim.

weeks.assessment_key: Kicking check (score each of 10 kicks on cues: plant foot beside ball, correct foot surface, follow through toward target): 4 = 4–5 accurate passes and 3+ shots on goal with all cues; 3 = 3 accurate passes, 2 shots on goal; 2 = 1–2 passes accurate or toe-kicking; 1 = no accurate kicks.

weeks.prep: Ball (soccer ball or playground ball), 4 cones for a small field and 2 more for goals. Invite a sibling, parent or friend for 2v1 and the mini game. Paper for Friday's reflection.
misconceptions: Everyone chasing the ball ('beehive soccer'). Teammates spread out into open space so they can receive a pass.
Facing the ball and standing still on defense. Use a ready stance (knees bent, on balls of feet) and stay between the attacker and the goal.

days.guide: Play 2-person keep-away in a square with one defender (parent). The child practices moving to open space — a spot where the passer has a clear lane — and calling for the ball. Freeze play occasionally and ask 'Where is the open space?'

questions.q: What is open space?
questions.a: An area away from defenders where a teammate can pass you the ball without it being intercepted.

questions.q: Why move after you pass?
questions.a: To get open again for a return pass.

days.guide: Teach the defensive stance: feet apart, knees bent, weight on balls of feet, arms out. The child shuffles to stay between the attacker and the goal as you dribble slowly.

questions.q: Where should a defender stand?
questions.a: Between the attacker and the goal they are protecting.

questions.q: Describe a good defensive stance.
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width apart, knees bent, on the balls of the feet, arms out, eyes on the attacker's body/ball.

days.guide: Play 2v1: two attackers try to score past one defender. Teach 'draw and pass': dribble at the defender, and when they come to you, pass to your open teammate.

questions.q: In 2v1, when should you pass?
questions.a: When the defender commits to you, pass to your teammate who is now open.

days.guide: Play a mini soccer or basketball game (2v2 or 3v3) for 15–20 minutes with simple rules. Pause to praise spacing, passing and fair play.

questions.q: What does fair play look like in a game?
questions.a: Following the rules, being honest about calls, no rough play, encouraging teammates and congratulating opponents.

days.guide: The child writes 3–5 sentences: one strategy they used (e.g., moving to open space, draw and pass, staying goal-side) and one fair-play moment.

questions.q: Give an example of a strategy and how it helped.
questions.a: E.g., 'I moved to open space so my brother could pass to me, and I scored.'

weeks.assessment_key: Game play observation and reflection rubric: 4 = during play the child moves to open space, uses a defensive stance goal-side, and passes when a teammate is open; reflection names a specific strategy, how it helped, and a specific fair-play moment; 3 = shows 2 of the 3 skills and reflection names a strategy and fair-play moment with less detail; 2 = mostly follows the ball, reflection vague; 1 = no reflection or unsafe play.

weeks.prep: Gather a paddle or short-handled racket (ping-pong paddle, paddleball or badminton racket), balloons and a tennis or foam ball. A flat wall such as a garage door for Thursday.
misconceptions: Swinging the whole arm wildly. Keep the paddle face flat and use small, controlled movements with a firm wrist.
Gripping too tight or holding the paddle at the end of the handle. Use a 'shake hands' grip close to the face for control.

days.guide: Teach the shake-hands grip. The child keeps a balloon up by tapping it gently with a flat paddle face, counting hits. Goal: 20 in a row.

questions.q: How do you hold the paddle?
questions.a: With a 'shake hands' grip, firm but relaxed.

days.guide: Bounce a ball upward on the paddle (paddle face flat, waist high), letting it rise only a few inches. Count consecutive hits in 3 trials.

questions.q: Why keep the paddle face flat?
questions.a: A flat face sends the ball straight up; a tilted face sends it sideways.

days.guide: Turn the paddle face down and 'dribble' the ball toward the ground while standing, then while walking slowly.

questions.q: How is a paddle down-dribble like a hand dribble?
questions.a: You push the ball down at a steady height and keep control while moving.

days.guide: Stand 6–8 feet from a wall. Drop the ball, let it bounce, hit it to the wall, let it bounce once, hit again. Count hits.

questions.q: How many bounces are allowed between wall hits?
questions.a: One.

days.guide: The child does 3 trials of up bounces and 3 of wall hits and records the best of each.

questions.q: Up bounce trials: 9, 15, 12. Best?

weeks.assessment_key: Paddle control counts: record best counts. Benchmarks for proficient: balloon 20 in a row, up bounces 10+, wall hits 5+ with one bounce between hits, with a flat paddle face and shake-hands grip. 4 = meets all benchmarks; 3 = meets 2; 2 = meets 1; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Paddle and ball, a wall, a rope or line on the ground as a 'net', and 2 hula hoops (or chalk circles) placed near and far.
misconceptions: Swinging down at the ball (chopping). Swing low to high to lift the ball over the net.
Facing the net. Turn the non-paddle side toward the target before swinging, just like the overhand throw.

days.guide: Teach forehand cues: 1) side to target (non-paddle shoulder toward the target), 2) swing low to high, 3) follow through toward the target and up. Shadow 20 swings, saying the cues.

questions.q: Name the 3 forehand cues.
questions.a: Side to target, swing low to high, follow through.

days.guide: Drop the ball beside the front foot, let it bounce, and hit a forehand to the wall 20 times. Count good hits that reach the wall above a chalk line.

questions.q: Where do you drop the ball for a drop hit?
questions.a: Out to the side and slightly in front of your body, on your paddle side.

days.guide: Rally over a rope or line with a partner, using forehands and counting hits in a row.

questions.q: Why swing low to high when hitting over a net?
questions.a: It lifts the ball up so it clears the net.

days.guide: Place hoops near and far. Hit forehands into each target, adjusting force: softer swing for near, firmer for far.

questions.q: How do you hit the far target?
questions.a: Use a bigger, firmer swing with more follow-through (more force).

days.guide: Forehand check: observe 5 forehands and score each on the 3 cues.

questions.q: Which foot is forward when a right-hander hits a forehand?
questions.a: The left foot (non-paddle side toward the target).

weeks.assessment_key: Forehand check: 5 hits × 3 cues = 15 points (side to target, low-to-high swing, follow through). 4 = 13–15 points; 3 = 10–12; 2 = 6–9; 1 = 0–5.

weeks.prep: Plastic bat, batting tee (or a tall cone), whiffle balls, and cones for left, center and right field. Mark a safety zone (a circle about 10 feet around the batter) where no one else may stand.
misconceptions: Hands apart or wrong hand on top. Right-handed batters put the left hand on the bottom, right hand on top, hands touching (stacked).
Throwing the bat after hitting. Drop or place the bat on the ground before running.

days.guide: Teach the grip (hands stacked, knuckles lined up, right-handers left hand on bottom) and side stance (feet shoulder-width, front shoulder toward the pitcher/tee, bat up). Take 20 dry swings with a level swing, stepping toward the target.

questions.q: For a right-handed batter, which hand goes on the bottom?
questions.a: The left hand.

questions.q: Which way does a batter face?
questions.a: Sideways, with the front shoulder pointing toward the pitcher/tee.

days.guide: Hit 20 balls off the tee at belly height, focusing on a level swing and following through. Count solid contacts.

questions.q: What is a level swing?
questions.a: A swing that moves flat across, through the ball, not chopping down or uppercutting.

days.guide: Show that hitting the ball earlier (out front) pulls it, and later sends it to the opposite field; open or close the stance to aim. Try to hit to left, center and right cones.

questions.q: If you turn your front foot slightly toward left field, where does the ball tend to go?
questions.a: Toward left field (for a right-handed batter).

days.guide: Mark the bat safety zone. Practice: check the zone is clear before swinging, then after hitting place the bat down and run. Practice 10 hit-and-place runs.

questions.q: What do you do with the bat after you hit?
questions.a: Drop or place it on the ground (never throw it) and run.

questions.q: Who can stand in the safety zone?
questions.a: Only the batter.

days.guide: Batting check: 10 swings off the tee, scored for contact and form (grip, stance, level swing, safe bat placement).

questions.q: Why do we place the bat instead of throwing it?
questions.a: A thrown bat can fly and hurt someone.

weeks.assessment_key: Batting check (10 hits): 1 point per solid contact (max 10) plus form points: correct stacked grip (1), side stance (1), level swing (1), bat placed safely each time (1). 4 = 7+ contacts and all 4 form points; 3 = 5–6 contacts and 3 form points; 2 = 3–4 contacts or 2 form points; 1 = fewer.

weeks.prep: Bat, tee, whiffle balls, paddles and a soft ball, bases (paper plates), cones for fielders; a score sheet.
misconceptions: Hitting straight to the fielder. Look for open space between or behind fielders and aim there.
Arguing calls. Agree on rules before playing and settle disagreements calmly (do-over or rock-paper-scissors).

days.guide: Play family whiffle ball with tee or soft underhand pitch: hit, run to first, simple outs (catch in air or ball to base before runner). Review bat safety.

questions.q: How can a fielder get a runner out?
questions.a: Catch the ball in the air, or get the ball to the base before the runner arrives (or tag the runner).

days.guide: Play paddle ball over a line: serve underhand, rally, and score a point when the ball lands in open space on the opponent's side.

questions.q: Where should you aim to score in paddle ball?
questions.a: Into open space away from your opponent.

days.guide: Place 2 fielders (cones or people). Discuss where the gaps are; the child tries to hit balls into the gaps and counts successes.

questions.q: Why place your hit away from fielders?
questions.a: So they can't catch it or field it quickly, giving you more time to run.

days.guide: The child chooses a striking game and keeps score fairly for the family, calling the score after each point.

questions.q: What does keeping score fairly mean?
questions.a: Counting points honestly for both sides and announcing the score accurately.

days.guide: Unit check: 5 paddle forehands to a target and 5 tee hits aimed at gaps.

questions.q: Name one cue that is the same for batting and the paddle forehand.
questions.a: Side to target (or step toward the target / follow through).

weeks.assessment_key: Striking unit check: paddle (5 forehands, 1 point each for landing in target zone with correct cues) + batting (5 tee hits, 1 point each for solid contact toward a gap) = 10. 4 = 9–10 plus fair, accurate scorekeeping; 3 = 7–8; 2 = 4–6; 1 = 0–3.

weeks.prep: Choose 4 songs with clearly different tempos (slow, medium, fast) that you have previewed for content. Clear space. For Thursday, choose a GoNoodle dance video (gonoodle.com, free account) and preview it.
misconceptions: Moving faster than the beat. Listen first and clap the steady beat before moving.
Thinking dance has to be fancy. Simple movements done on the beat with changes in level and direction make a strong dance.

days.guide: Play each song; first clap the steady beat, then march, then step side to side to it. Discuss which songs are fast (high tempo) and slow.

questions.q: What is tempo?
questions.a: How fast or slow the beat of the music is.

questions.q: How do you find the beat?
questions.a: Listen for the steady pulse and clap or tap along to it.

days.guide: Call 'high' (on tiptoes, arms up), 'middle' (standing normal), 'low' (crouched, near the floor) while dancing; switch every 8 counts.

questions.q: Name the 3 levels in dance.
questions.a: High, middle and low.

days.guide: Face each other; the leader moves in slow motion and the follower mirrors exactly, like a reflection. Switch every minute.

questions.q: If the leader raises their right arm, which arm does the mirror raise?
questions.a: Their left arm (like a reflection in a mirror).

days.guide: Watch the GoNoodle dance once, then follow along twice, then try to do parts without watching.

questions.q: How do you learn a dance from a video?
questions.a: Watch first, follow along, then practice small parts until you can do them without looking.

days.guide: Count '1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8' to the music. The child creates 8 counts of movement (e.g., 4 steps right, 2 claps, a turn) and performs it 3 times in a row on the beat.

questions.q: How many counts in a dance phrase like ours?
questions.a: 8 counts.

weeks.assessment_key: 8-count phrase rubric: 4 = original 8-count phrase performed on the beat, repeated 3 times the same way, uses at least 2 levels; 3 = on the beat with small changes between repeats; 2 = off the beat often or fewer than 8 counts; 1 = cannot create a phrase.

weeks.prep: Find instrumental music for each dance (a lively fiddle reel for the Virginia Reel and the traditional Jarabe Tapatío music, both widely available) and a short video of each to preview. Need at least 2 people for the reel (more is better).
misconceptions: Thinking the Mexican Hat Dance is just about a hat. The Jarabe Tapatío is Mexico's national folk dance from Jalisco; the hat comes from the part where the man's sombrero is placed on the ground and the woman dances around its brim.
Thinking folk dances were made up recently or by one person. Folk dances grow out of the traditions of a community and are passed down over generations.

days.guide: Teach Virginia Reel figures in two facing lines: forward and back (4 steps in, 4 out), right-hand turn, left-hand turn, two-hand turn, do-si-do (pass right shoulders, back to back, return). Then the head couple sashays down the middle and back.

questions.q: What is a do-si-do?
questions.a: Partners walk forward, pass right shoulders, step side by side back to back, and walk backward to their places without turning around.

days.guide: Teach the basic heel-toe pattern: hop slightly and touch the right heel forward, then the left heel, then a quick three-step stamp (zapateado) pattern. Practice slowly counting aloud.

questions.q: Which country does the Jarabe Tapatío come from?
questions.a: Mexico (the state of Jalisco).

days.guide: Practice each dance to music, counting steps aloud. Slow the music or count slowly at first.

questions.q: Why count aloud when learning a dance?
questions.a: It keeps the steps matched to the beat and helps you remember the order.

days.guide: Share background: the Virginia Reel is an American country dance with roots in English and Scottish reels, popular in colonial and pioneer times at social gatherings. The Jarabe Tapatío is Mexico's national dance from Jalisco ('tapatío' means from Guadalajara), a courtship dance performed at celebrations and fiestas. Find both places on a map.

questions.q: Where do the roots of the Virginia Reel come from?
questions.a: English and Scottish country dances (reels), brought to America.

questions.q: Why are folk dances danced?
questions.a: To celebrate and share a community's culture at gatherings, festivals and holidays.

days.guide: Perform both dances for family. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Tell your audience one fact about each dance.
questions.a: Virginia Reel: American country dance from English/Scottish reels; Jarabe Tapatío: Mexico's national dance from Jalisco.

weeks.assessment_key: Folk dance performance rubric: 4 = performs the main figures of the Virginia Reel (forward and back, turns, do-si-do) and the Jarabe heel-toe steps in order and on the beat, and states where each dance comes from; 3 = most figures correct with a few prompts; 2 = needs frequent prompts or off beat; 1 = cannot perform figures.

weeks.prep: Preview recordings of the 'Cha-Cha Slide' and an Electric Slide song (radio edits are fine; check content). Clear space with room to step 4 steps in each direction. Timer and heart-rate log.
misconceptions: Crossing in front in the grapevine. The trailing foot crosses behind the leading foot.
Turning the wrong way in a line dance. In the Electric Slide, the quarter turn goes to the left so the group faces a new wall each time.

days.guide: Teach the grapevine to the right: step right to the side (1), left foot crosses behind (2), step right to the side (3), touch left beside right (4); then reverse to the left (5–8). Practice slowly, then to music.

questions.q: In a grapevine to the right, where does the left foot cross?
questions.a: Behind the right foot.

questions.q: How many counts is a grapevine right and left?
questions.a: 8 counts (4 right, 4 left).

days.guide: Play the Cha-Cha Slide; the song calls out each move, so the child listens and responds (slides, hops, stomps, cha-cha). Practice the moves without music first, then with it.

questions.q: Why is the Cha-Cha Slide easy to learn?
questions.a: The song tells you which move to do next, so you just listen and follow the calls.

days.guide: Teach the Electric Slide pattern: grapevine right, grapevine left, walk back 3 and touch, rock forward and back, then a quarter turn to the left and repeat facing the new wall.

questions.q: After one full pattern, which way do you face?
questions.a: A new wall, a quarter turn to the left.

days.guide: Take resting heart rate. Dance 3 songs in a row, then immediately take a 15-second pulse × 4 and compare.

questions.q: Resting 84 bpm; after dancing you count 33 in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate and how much did it rise?
Is line dancing exercise? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes — your heart rate and breathing go up, which works your heart and lungs.

days.guide: The child performs the Electric Slide (or Cha-Cha Slide) start to finish without you calling the steps.

questions.q: What is a line dance?
questions.a: A dance where people stand in lines and do the same steps at the same time, often turning to face new walls.

weeks.assessment_key: Line dance performance rubric: 4 = performs a full line dance with correct steps in order, on the beat, with correct turns and no cues; 3 = one or two small errors, recovers quickly; 2 = needs some cues; 1 = needs cues throughout.

weeks.prep: Help the child choose a song (instrumental works well) about 1 minute long. Paper for the dance plan. Review vocabulary: levels (high/middle/low), pathways (straight/curved/zigzag), tempo, force (strong/light).
misconceptions: Making each part different with no repetition. Repeating a phrase gives the dance structure, like a chorus in a song.
Forgetting the beginning and ending shapes. A dance starts and ends with a still shape to frame it.

days.guide: Choose a song and theme (ocean, storm, animals). Brainstorm 4 movement ideas that match the theme and name the level and pathway for each (e.g., waves = low, curved pathway).

questions.q: How could you show a storm with force?
questions.a: Strong, sharp, fast movements (stamping, quick arm slashes) — and a calm part with light, slow movements.

questions.q: Give a movement idea that uses a low level.
questions.a: E.g., crawling like a crab or rolling like a wave close to the floor.

days.guide: Build a 32-count dance: beginning shape, three 8-count phrases, and an ending shape (the shapes and phrases add up to 32 counts — e.g., 4 counts start shape, 3 × 8 phrases, 4 counts end shape). Write it in a chart.

questions.q: How many 8-count phrases fit in 32 counts?
If your start and end shapes take 4 counts each, how many counts are left for phrases?
questions.a: 32 − 8 = 24, which is 3 phrases of 8.

days.guide: Rehearse 5 times. Add one tempo change (e.g., slow-motion phrase) and one level change.

questions.q: What is a tempo change in dance?
questions.a: Moving faster or slower than before (e.g., switching to slow motion).

days.guide: Perform for family, then teach them one phrase by demonstrating and counting.

questions.q: How do you teach a phrase to someone?
questions.a: Show it, break it into small parts with counts, do it together, then let them try alone.

days.guide: The child describes how they used force, levels and pathways and what they would change next time.

questions.q: Describe one place in your dance you used a curved pathway.
questions.a: Answer should name a specific part, e.g., 'I skipped in a circle during phrase 2 to show swirling water.'

weeks.assessment_key: Original dance rubric: 4 = 32 counts with beginning and ending shapes, 3 phrases matching the theme, uses all 3 levels, at least 2 pathways, a tempo change and clear force changes; child explains choices; 3 = most elements present, one missing; 2 = dance is short or unclear and few elements; 1 = no planned dance.

weeks.prep: Gather a hula hoop, an old blanket or tarp, 3 balloons, a blindfold or scarf, and soft 'mines' (shoes, pillows, cones). Gather 3+ family members. Timer for each challenge.
misconceptions: Thinking the fastest person should do all the work. Teamwork means every member has a role and the group plans together.
Thinking cooperative games have no winner so effort doesn't matter. The team competes against the clock or a goal, so everyone's effort counts.

days.guide: Stand in a circle holding hands. Pass the hula hoop all the way around by stepping through it without letting go of hands. Time 3 rounds and talk about strategies that made it faster.

questions.q: What strategy helped your team get faster?
questions.a: E.g., talking/helping each other, dipping a shoulder, the next person getting ready early.

days.guide: Everyone stands on the blanket. Without anyone stepping off, the group flips the blanket over. Plan first, then try.

questions.q: Why is planning before trying important?
questions.a: It gives everyone a role and an idea so the team works together instead of guessing.

days.guide: Keep 3 balloons in the air for 60 seconds using only assigned body parts (e.g., elbows, heads, knees). Restart the timer if one touches the ground.

questions.q: What did you do when a balloon was about to fall near someone else?
questions.a: Called out to warn them or moved to help, while keeping my own balloon up.

days.guide: Set up 'minefield': one partner is blindfolded, the other guides them through the mines using only words. Switch. Discuss trust and clear directions.

questions.q: What makes a good guide?
questions.a: Clear, calm, specific directions ('two small steps forward, stop, step left'), and keeping your partner safe.

questions.q: Why is trust important in this game?
questions.a: The blindfolded partner can't see and must believe the guide will keep them safe.

days.guide: Repeat the fastest challenge, time it, and have the child name encouraging words that helped.

questions.q: Name two encouraging things teammates said.
questions.a: E.g., 'You've got this,' 'Nice job,' 'Almost there,' 'Let's try again.'

weeks.assessment_key: Team challenge rubric: 4 = participates fully, shares an idea in planning, uses encouraging words, follows safety rules, and names specific encouraging words; 3 = participates and encourages others with prompting; 2 = participates but discourages others or ignores the plan; 1 = refuses to participate.

weeks.prep: Belt flags or scarves tucked into waistbands, cones for boundaries and lanes, two 'flags' (bandanas) for capture the flag; invite friends or siblings if possible.
misconceptions: Running straight at a tagger. Use fakes, quick changes of direction and open space.
Thinking an honest call loses the game. Honesty keeps the game fair and fun, and others will trust you.

days.guide: Tuck a flag in each side of the waistband. Players try to pull others' flags while protecting their own, using open space. A pulled flag means do 5 jumping jacks and rejoin.

questions.q: How do you avoid taggers in flag tag?
questions.a: Move into open space away from them, keep your eyes up and change direction quickly.

questions.q: Is it fair to hold your flag with your hand?
questions.a: No — you protect it by moving, not by holding or blocking it.

days.guide: Set a cone lane. A defender stands in the middle; the child gets past using a fake (lean one way, go the other), a pivot, or a change of speed.

questions.q: Name 3 dodging moves.
questions.a: Fake, pivot (turn on one foot), change of speed (and change of direction).

days.guide: Play capture the flag: two territories, a flag at the back of each. Plan roles: defenders guard, attackers try to grab the opposing flag. Tagged players go to 'jail' until freed.

questions.q: Why have both offense and defense players?
questions.a: So you can try to capture the other flag while still protecting your own.

days.guide: Role-play situations: you feel a tag but no one saw; the score is close and you step out of bounds. Practice saying 'I was tagged' or 'I was out.'

questions.q: Why does honesty keep games fun?
questions.a: Everyone trusts the game is fair, there are fewer arguments, and people want to keep playing together.

days.guide: Write a 3–5 sentence reflection: which strategy helped your team most and why, with an example.

questions.q: Give an example of a team strategy in capture the flag.
questions.a: E.g., two players run at once so defenders can't guard both; one gets the flag.

weeks.assessment_key: Strategy reflection rubric: 4 = names a specific strategy (e.g., fake, use open space, split offense/defense), explains why it worked with an example from play, and mentions fair play; 3 = names a strategy with a basic reason; 2 = vague ("we ran fast"); 1 = no reflection.

weeks.prep: Balloon or beach ball, a rope tied between two chairs at about the child's head height as a net, a playground ball, chalk to draw a four-square court (4 squares, each about 5–6 feet), and a wall.
misconceptions: Hitting the balloon with a fist. Use two-hand volleys with fingers spread and slightly bent, pushing up.
Catching or holding the ball in four square. Hit it with an open palm; no catching or carrying.

days.guide: Teach the two-hand volley: hands above forehead in a triangle shape, fingers spread, push up. Rally a balloon over the rope net, counting team hits.

questions.q: Where should your hands be for a volley?
questions.a: Above your forehead, fingers spread like holding a big ball, pushing up and out.

days.guide: Teach four square rules: the ball bounces once in your square, then you hit it with an open palm (underhand) to another square; you are out if it bounces twice, you miss, or you hit it out of bounds. The server is in the highest square (4 or 'king').

questions.q: When are you out in four square?
questions.a: If the ball bounces twice in your square, you hit it out of bounds or on a line (by your rules), or you don't hit it after it bounces in your square.

questions.q: How do you hit the ball in four square?
questions.a: With an open palm (or both hands), underhand, after one bounce — no catching.

days.guide: Partners take turns hitting a playground ball against a wall after one bounce, alternating hits. Count the longest rally.

questions.q: Why is moving your feet important in a rally?
questions.a: It gets you in position behind the ball so you can make a controlled hit.

days.guide: Play 2v2 over the net with a balloon or beach ball, aiming for open spaces on the other side; up to 3 team hits per side.

questions.q: Where should you aim to win the point?
questions.a: Into open space where the other team isn't standing.

days.guide: Skill check: 10 two-hand volleys to a partner, counting controlled ones (reach the partner and are catchable).

questions.q: Out of 10 volleys, 8 reached your partner. What percent is that?
